meta.title: Conflict Watchlist
meta.notes: Fully automated register: a scheduled open-source review rewrites this file daily (procedure in docs/WATCHLIST-REVIEW.md) and an hourly GitHub Action refreshes the live reporting feed (watchlist-live.json) from GDELT. Every comparison the dashboard shows (state moves, changed dimensions, the attention-score bonuses) is made against the register as it stood compareDays (7) days ago, taken from each item's `snapshots` (one entry per review: date, state and the five dimensions). Each review: (1) set reviewDate/previousReviewDate, (2) for every item set the new `now` on the five dimensions and the new `state`, then append today's snapshot (keep the last 60), (3) rewrite `status` (`summary`: plain-language current status whose first sentence states the newest development; `sources`: 2–3 links to the newest reporting), `whyNow`, `topic` and `whyMatters` (stable framing, revise only on a phase change), `changes` (dated bullets covering the last 7 days: keep those still inside the window, add today's, drop older ones), `next`, `ignore` and `sources`, (4) record any state move in `history` and keep `timeline` (4–8 dated one-line events of the current phase, chronological) current. The dashboard derives attention rank, movements, changed-dimension flags, staleness, coverage surges — do not type those in. `next` holds named, checkable indicators.

Priority.desc: Direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value.

Active.desc: Material trend, escalation, or regional relevance.

Archive.desc: Reserve — retained for reference and pattern work; revisit only on a named trigger.

phase.label: Conflict phase
phase.desc: A short label for the stage the conflict is in (for example attritional war, ceasefire without implementation, grey-zone contest). It sits under the current-status summary and shows the label from 7 days ago when it changed.

escalation.label: Escalation risk
escalation.desc: How likely a step up in intensity or a change of phase is in the coming weeks.

levels.Low: Stable; no live trigger and restraints hold.
levels.Moderate: Triggers exist (deadlines, disputes, incidents) but restraints are holding.
levels.High: Active exchanges or a named trigger that is likely to fire; a phase change is plausible within weeks.
levels.Severe: Active war or ongoing kinetic exchange with strategic stakes (major shipping lanes, energy, great-power forces).

tempo.label: Operational tempo
tempo.desc: How much military activity is actually happening in the review window.

levels.Medium: Recurring incidents or steady, limited operations (patrols, fortification, occasional strikes).
levels.High: Daily strikes or operations across fronts.

adaptation.label: Adaptation behaviour
adaptation.desc: How much new tactical or technical behaviour appeared in the window; this is where the Army learning sits.

levels.Low: Both sides are using the same methods as before.
levels.High: Novel, repeatable adaptations appeared (new weapons employment, counter-measures, doctrine shifts).

sgExposure.label: Singapore exposure
sgExposure.desc: How directly the conflict touches Singapore's interests. Not shown as a register column; it still feeds the attention score and the expanded row.

levels.Moderate: An ASEAN or diplomatic role, observer contributions, or supply-chain spillover.
levels.High: Direct effect on sea lanes, energy or shipping, a Singapore-flagged vessel affected, or relevance to deployments.

attentionScore.desc: Deterministic, explainable rank. state (Priority 40 / Active 25 / Watch 10 / Archive 0) + escalation risk (Severe 20 / High 15 / Moderate 8 / Low 2) + 5 per dimension that changed over the last 7 days (compareDays) + 10 if the state moved up over the same window + Singapore exposure (High 8 / Moderate 4 / Low 0) + tier (T1 6 / T2 3 / T3 0) + 8 if the live open-source feed shows a coverage surge (see definitions.feed.surgeRule). Items flagged ignore-for-now are shown but ranked last.

feed.source: GDELT DOC 2.0 API (open, no key). Per item: 30-day daily article counts (TimelineVolRaw) and the most relevant English-language articles of the last 7 days (ArtList, HybridRel). Synced by .github/workflows/sync-watchlist-feed.yml into watchlist-live.json.
feed.surgeRule: A coverage surge is flagged when the last 7 days carry at least twice the article volume of the 7 days before and at least 20 articles; a surge adds 8 points to the attention score.
feed.titleFilter: Articles are kept only when the title contains one of the item's terms, to cut GDELT's full-text noise.
feed.terms: Title filter: at least one of these substrings must appear in an article title for it to count as reporting on the item.
feed.require: Optional groups of substrings; a title must contain at least one term from every group (two-party theatres: one term per side).
feed.exclude: Optional substrings that drop a title (sport, entertainment and other noise), in addition to the sync's global list.
feed.spamDomainsNote: Article sources dropped outright (livestream/score spam). The daily review adds domains seen producing noise.

columns.tier: Standing relevance to the Army: T1 Priority Conflicts, T2 Active Regional & Escalation Watches, T3 Baseline Regional Research Reserve. Tiers do not change week to week.
columns.state: Today's monitoring state: Priority (direct strategic relevance or high Army learning value), Active (material trend, escalation or regional relevance), Watch (baseline monitoring), Archive (reserve; revisit on a named trigger). ▲▼ marks a move over the last 7 days.
columns.status: Current status: the newest title-matched headline from the live open-source feed (synced hourly) on top, then a plain-language summary of what is happening now whose first sentence states the newest development, with links to the newest reporting it rests on. The phase label sits beneath; a struck-through label is the phase 7 days ago.
columns.coverage: Open-source coverage from the live feed (GDELT with Google News fallback): the sparkline is the last 30 days (or four weekly counts), the number is articles in the last 7 days with the change against the 7 before. 'Surge' = at least twice the prior week and at least 20 articles. Refreshes hourly.
columns.nextIndicator: The soonest dated indicator to watch, tagged with the numbered topic and watch area it informs (or 'cross-cutting' when it bears on the theatre as a whole). Expand the row for the full list.
columns.confidence: How well-sourced the assessment is: High (multiple independent, dated sources), Medium (some single-source or snippet-only items), Low (thin or contested reporting).
columns.attention: Attention score, the register's sort order. Hover a score for its breakdown.
columns.topic: Topics of interest: the three capability contests the Army follows this theatre for, set by the team (from the watchlist workbook). Numbered so they line up with the 'Why it matters' and 'Watch areas' columns; the chip is the topic's adaptability rating.
columns.whyMatters: Why it matters here: for each numbered topic, what the theatre tests (the capability, behaviour or mechanism under study).
columns.watchAreas: Watch areas: for each numbered topic, its watch status and what to monitor. Status tags: Rising (activity increasing), Established (steady pattern), Contested (the outcome is still open), Watch for trigger (review only on a named event), Background monitor, Declining.
columns.adaptability: Adaptability: how transferable the topic's lessons are to the Army — High, Medium or Low, set by the team.

watches.desc: Watches follow one operational thread of an item on its own once a trigger event makes it worth it, as a record of tactical lessons: which tactics and actions succeeded, which failed and which were superseded, on both sides, with dated evidence. Two kinds: a shadow-war watch (kind "shadow-war": sabotage, incursions, cable damage, jamming and other attacks below the threshold of war, and the defenders' countermeasures) and an operation watch (kind "operation": one named military operation). Each carries a narrower daily feed, plus dated findings and an assessment researched from open sources at each review.

types.succeeded: The tactic or action achieved its aim, on the evidence available (ground taken and held, target hit, intrusion undetected or unanswered, threat intercepted, cell caught before acting).
types.failed: The tactic or action did not achieve its aim or was defeated (attack repulsed, objective abandoned, intruder shot down, perpetrators caught with little effect).
types.superseded: The tactic or plan was replaced by a newer method or made obsolete by a countermeasure (a plan scaled back, a weapon or approach overtaken).
types.contested: The outcome is unclear or disputed: claims not yet confirmed, sources disagree, or it is too early to judge.

items.whyNow: Ukraine's collapse of a Kerch Bridge road span on 17 Nov, set against Russia's repeated strikes on Kyiv's Dnipro bridges, is the sharpest test yet of whether sustained strikes on crossings can shape a ground front that is otherwise static. The Trump–Xi–Putin declaration in Shenzhen on 19 Nov said nothing about Ukraine, so the strike war, not diplomacy, still sets the winter terms.
changes: 19 Nov: Trump, Xi and Putin held their first trilateral meeting in Shenzhen and issued a four-point declaration on UN reform, refined-fuel supply, official immunities and nuclear-risk dialogue that said nothing about the Russia–Ukraine war; Ukraine's backers met in Berlin in parallel (CFR).

18 Nov: Russia launched 141 drones, 73 of them jet-powered, overnight and struck a residential area of Odesa and then the responders; Ukraine hit the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries in Krasnodar Krai and a Siverskyi Donets road bridge at Stanytsia Luhanska; ISW put November Russian losses at about 2,269 a day and reported a Rzeczpospolita account of a foiled Russian false-flag plot near Kaliningrad (single source) (ISW).

17 Nov: A second night of strikes using Neptune missiles, FP-5 Flamingo, Ruta and drones collapsed a road span and arch of the Kerch Bridge, halting road traffic while rail continued; Russia claimed 1,441 drones downed and hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges, cutting heating to hundreds of Left Bank buildings (TWZ, Al Jazeera).

16 Nov: Ukrainian fixed-wing drones first struck the Kerch Bridge overnight, Russia hit Zaporizhzhia's Preobrazhenskyi Bridge, likely Russian uncrewed surface vessels sank the merchant ship Betul 8 in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, and Starshield speed caps hampering interceptor drones entered a seventh day (ISW).

14 Nov: Zelensky said US negotiators had floated NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for withdrawal from Donbas and rejected Russia's proposed local ceasefire in Kostiantynivka; ISW reported a ground-launched Dan-T loitering munition and Russian armour using fog to push into the kill zone, and Ukrainian strikes on Lipetsk-2 air base and a Samara oil station (ISW).

timeline.text: Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps revealed Operation Vivaldi, a counteroffensive near Lyman it said cleared 75 square kilometres of Russian infiltrators and liberated Serednie and nearby villages.

Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at energy sites around Kyiv and Kharkiv, leaving 600,000 without power, as the 3rd Army Corps claimed a fourth Vivaldi stage of 101 square kilometres north of Lyman.

Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting fires at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and Ruchi depot and hitting a VK data centre about 850 km from the border, its deepest mass raid of the war.

A limited humanitarian ceasefire around occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast took effect for aid deliveries and evacuations, the first agreed local truce of the year, while Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles and 280 drones.
Russian glide bombs, including a FAB-3000, struck a school used as a humanitarian aid point in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and then a nearby shelter, killing at least 40 people.

Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones, all the missiles aimed at Kyiv and its region, hitting the city's Northern Bridge four times and a substation linking two nuclear plants to central Ukraine.
US-mediated trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi ended after two days with agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange but no ceasefire and no movement on territory.
A second night of Ukrainian drone and missile strikes collapsed a road span and arch of the Kerch Bridge, halting road traffic between Russia and occupied Crimea while rail service continued.

text: On persistent ISR versus signature management and deception, the Established and Contested status is borne out. ISW reported on 13 and 14 Nov that Russian armour, some fitted with active protection, is using fog and rain to push into the drone kill zone, and on 18 Nov that bad weather enabled larger assaults near Slovyansk, yet neither side advanced that day and ISW still counts 41 Ukrainian positions around Kostiantynivka, so weather buys windows rather than durable gains. On EW versus alternative UAS control and layered counter-UAS, the Rising status holds: Russia fielded a ground-launched Dan-T (14 Nov), more fibre-optic Molniya-2 drones and its 41st Unmanned Systems Brigade (18 Nov), while Starshield speed caps were in a seventh day on 16 Nov against salvos of 73 jet drones, weakening Ukraine's interceptor layer.

On contested sustainment versus dispersed support and repair, the Established and Contested status hardens into a mutual campaign against crossings. Ukraine collapsed a Kerch Bridge road span on 17 Nov and hit a Siverskyi Donets bridge on 17–18 Nov, which ISW expects to push Russia onto the land route north of the Azov Sea, while Russia struck Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges on 17 Nov and Zaporizhzhia's on 16 Nov. Rail still running across Kerch shows redundancy blunting single-node strikes, so repeated targeting, not one blow, is the variable to watch.

watches.title: Russia–Europe shadow-war watch: tactics and countermeasures
watches.trigger: Russian helicopter and drone incursions into Poland, Romania and Moldova, 23–24 Sep 2026
watches.question: Which Russian tactics below the threshold of open war against Europe (drone and aircraft incursions, sabotage and arson through recruited proxies, undersea cable and pipeline damage, shadow-fleet operations, GPS jamming, cyber attacks with real-world effect) are succeeding, which are failing or being countered, and which have been superseded; and how are European and NATO countermeasures (air policing and counter-drone defence, rules of engagement, maritime interdiction, arrests and expulsions) adapting?

findings.actor: Polish government, police, Border Guard and army
findings.tactic: Public threat disclosure and border surge
findings.text: Rzeczpospolita reported on 18 Nov 2026, citing government and intelligence sources, that the plot Poland's 2-15 Nov Kaliningrad-border operation was guarding against was never executed; special services coordinator Siemoniak would not confirm a false flag but said the deployment answered a real threat. ISW assesses that Tusk's public warnings and the surge of police, counter-terrorism and army units likely deterred or disrupted the operation, an assessment rather than proof of deterrence.

findings.tactic: False-flag cross-border attack disguised as Ukrainians
findings.text: Rzeczpospolita reported on 18 Nov 2026 that Russian-linked personnel disguised as Ukrainians were to attack from Poland into Kaliningrad Oblast in late October or early November, a mass-casualty provocation meant to cut aid to Ukraine, after an influx of Russian intelligence officers into Kaliningrad. The attack did not take place; the account rests on unnamed Polish sources relayed by ISW (single source).

findings.tactic: Drone overflights of Moldova during Ukraine strikes
findings.text: On the evening of 17 Nov 2026 seven drones violated Moldovan airspace, one flying over Chisinau according to President Sandu; the defence ministry said five crashed near villages, a sixth possibly in Ocnita and a seventh vanished from radar near Leova heading for Romania, and civilian flights were briefly suspended. No drone was reported shot down, so the incursion again achieved disruption without interception; Russia denies its drones enter Moldova.

findings.tactic: Arresting contract saboteurs and closing border
findings.text: Estonia's chief prosecutor said on 15 Nov 2026 that eight Latvian residents had been detained over the Threod Systems attack, which Prime Minister Michal attributed to Russian intelligence, and Tallinn announced it will close its border crossings with Russia from 1 Dec. The swift arrests contained the attack; whether closing the crossings stops recruitment of disposable proxies from third countries is untested.

findings.actor: Romanian government with France and NATO
findings.tactic: Maritime patrols and counter-drone help request
findings.text: After the 13-14 Nov drone strikes off Sulina, Romania's PM said fighters were scrambled twice but no interception was reported; on 15 Nov the defence minister sought allied surveillance patrols and counter-drone equipment at the NATO ministers' meeting, France moved an Atlantique 2 maritime patrol aircraft to Romania and a Sulina-Sfantu Gheorghe sea area was declared dangerous for navigation. Whether the added surveillance prevents further strikes is not yet tested.

findings.tactic: Drone strikes on merchant ships off Sulina
findings.text: Late on 13 Nov 2026 drones hit the cargo ship Larissa 1 and late on 14 Nov the tankers Evia Petrol V and Ali Najafov and the bulk carrier Marsol near Romania's Sulina canal, two of them inside Romanian territorial waters; fires were put out and no one was hurt, Reuters reported. ISW calls Evia Petrol V the first NATO-flagged vessel struck; the strikes landed despite two fighter scrambles, while the drones' origin is unconfirmed and Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbours.

findings.actor: Russian intelligence (per Estonian PM); eight Latvian-resident proxies
findings.tactic: Explosive arson attack on drone maker
findings.text: In the early hours of 14 Nov 2026 an attempt to cause an explosion and fire hit Threod Systems, a drone maker near Tallinn, following the August arson at Milrem Robotics. PM Michal said heightened security and a swift police reaction averted extensive damage and the attackers were detained; the GRU attribution rests on Estonian officials, who have not shown their evidence.

findings.actor: Unidentified drones from Belarus; Lithuanian crisis centre and NATO air policing
findings.tactic: Drone incursions from Belarus closing airports
findings.text: On the night of 10-11 Nov 2026 suspected drones from Belarus triggered two air alerts, one rising to red with residents told to shelter, and Vilnius and Kaunas airports were temporarily closed, disrupting three flights and more than 400 passengers; Latvia activated drone interceptors as one drone crossed into its airspace. NATO jets were scrambled twice and detected an object but did not shoot it down, so the disruption worked and interception again did not; no operator has been identified (single source).

findings.actor: Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) National Cyberint Center
findings.text: SRI disclosed on 11 Nov 2026 that Turla, a group linked to Russia's FSB, had breached an unnamed Romanian government body in December 2025 by exploiting Microsoft vulnerabilities, using malware ESET says hunts for NATO and EU emails. SRI says its Cyberint centre stopped the attack with EU and NATO partners, no exfiltration of sensitive data was found and the email service was fixed; the result rests on SRI's own account.

findings.tactic: Arresting paid arson and reconnaissance cell
findings.text: Poland's ABW arrested two Ukrainians aged 24 and 25, announced on 10 Nov 2026, suspected of photographing critical infrastructure and military sites, setting cars on fire and swapping in Ukrainian military number plates, for pay partly in cryptocurrency on behalf of Russian intelligence. The car arsons had already happened, but the cell is now in three-month custody facing 10 years to life, the latest in a run of Polish and German roll-ups of disposable proxy agents.

findings.actor: UK Counter Terrorism Policing with the FBI and US military
findings.tactic: Arrest of NATO-corps officer for espionage
findings.text: On 10 Nov 2026 British counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old US Army officer serving with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, which US and UK officials linked to Russia, under the National Security Act. Searches continue and no allegation has been detailed, so whether a penetration of an allied headquarters was cut off or already did damage is unknown.

findings.actor: Unidentified senders (signed 'Male State' and 'Mikhail Andropov'; no state attribution)
findings.tactic: Mass hoax bomb threats against flights
findings.text: From 2 to 6 Nov 2026 emailed bomb threats hit flights and airports across Europe, disrupting at least 30 flights on 5 Nov with diversions and fighter escorts, and on 6 Nov reached RTE, Nova TV and Sky News, forcing RTE to evacuate its Dublin headquarters; the emails demanded an end to aid for Ukraine. All were hoaxes, but the low-cost tactic achieved repeated disruption; Spain called it hybrid aggression while no state has been named and Male State's founder denied involvement.

assessment.text: Between 6 and 19 Nov cheap stand-off tools kept working while close-in sabotage kept failing. Drones hit four merchant ships off Sulina on 13-14 Nov, two inside Romanian waters, despite two fighter scrambles, and seven drones crossed Moldova on 17 Nov with none shot down, repeating the uninterrupted Belarus drone closures of Lithuanian airports on 10-11 Nov; Romania's answer, maritime patrols and a request for counter-drone kit on 15 Nov, is untested. Physical sabotage is being countered: the 14 Nov explosive arson at Estonia's Threod Systems was averted and eight Latvian-resident proxies detained, Estonia will close its Russian border crossings on 1 Dec, and Poland's 2-15 Nov border surge coincided with a reported false-flag raid from Poland into Kaliningrad that was never executed, which ISW thinks deterrence by disclosure helped stop (single source). Russia is adapting by recruiting third-country proxies and shifting to drones and deniable maritime strikes rather than cable sabotage, which NATO says Baltic Sentry has displaced.

timeline.text: Thailand and Cambodia signed a ceasefire taking effect at noon, ending 20 days of fighting that killed over 100 people and displaced more than half a million.
Thailand's armed forces chief announced completion of the first 1.3 km of a permanent concrete border wall in Chanthaburi's Pong Nam Ron district, with over 7 km more planned.

The Hague conciliation round closed with the first agreed confidence-building measures (a direct channel between the two navies among them, by Thailand's account), while the Commission noted earlier measures were unimplemented and set a third meeting in Kuala Lumpur for 24–27 November.

Cambodia's culture ministry demanded the return of artefacts Thailand removed from K'nar temple and called Thai activity at disputed border temples a fait accompli, as the Thai army rejected Cambodian charges that its barbed-wire barriers were redrawing the boundary by force.

Thailand's defence minister said the boundary dispute was unresolved, parked defence-ministry talks in favour of the Regional Border Committee, and said troops facing Cambodian soldiers climbing Hill 642 apply rules of engagement starting with dialogue and warning shots.

The ASEAN Observer Team visited the Chey Chomneas checkpoint area in Pursat, where Cambodia said Thai forces had moved an observation post about 20 metres forward and kept digging trenches, and the team inspected a bridge destroyed by Thai airstrikes in December 2025.

Hun Manet opened the Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh by calling the ceasefire fragile and proposing a Francophone mediation network, and the summit closed on 16 November with leaders backing Cambodia's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Thailand's foreign ministry rejected Cambodian claims of Thai occupation made at the Francophonie and ASEAN meetings and said Cambodia's conduct ran counter to the confidence-building measures agreed in October.

text: On border incident management versus escalation prevention, the Declining / cautiously improving status is borne out on the ground but not in rhetoric: no exchange of fire, warning-shot incident or mine casualty was reported from 6 to 19 Nov, while Hun Manet called the ceasefire fragile on 15 Nov and Cambodia charged on 17 Nov that Thai ordnance still contaminates about 3,800 sq km of seven provinces (Cambodian account). Restraint rests on rules of engagement and a closed border, not a settlement. On ceasefire monitoring versus local force autonomy, the trigger has not fired; the last observer-recorded consolidation remains the Thai post moved forward at Chey Chomneas on 5 Nov, and no observer findings were published this week.

On regional mediation versus bilateral military signalling, the Background monitor status is contradicted: the contest has shifted into forums. Cambodia secured Francophonie backing for its territorial integrity on 16 Nov, Thailand replied the same day that this breached the October confidence-building measures, and Trump pledged on 17 Nov to uphold the ceasefire. Mediation is multiplying rather than converging, which makes the 24–27 Nov conciliation round a test of whether lawfare contains or feeds the land dispute. Adaptability stays Low.

timeline.text: US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and his wife in overnight strikes across Caracas and three other states, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges.

Opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela overland from Colombia after about ten months abroad, greeted by tens of thousands of supporters on the road to Caracas.

text: On counter-criminal operations versus sovereignty and escalation, the trigger-led status is now carried by consent rather than coercion: Hegseth’s 18 Nov agreement in Caracas formalises joint training and intelligence sharing with the government whose 30 Oct Apure raid reportedly drew on US support, while no new strike on Venezuelan soil was found. The sovereignty question has moved from unilateral force to an institutionalised partnership whose scope and troop footprint are undefined. On border and maritime control versus illicit networks, the Established status holds but the pressure sits in Colombia: a 12 Nov drone attack in Tibú killed four soldiers, with investigators examining whether the drones were flown from Venezuela (single source), and no lethal US boat strike was found, while a 17 Nov lawsuit by Ecuadorian fishermen challenged an unacknowledged strike (single source).

On information operations versus political legitimacy, the Rising status is only partly borne out: the fourth round opened on 13 Nov and by 19 Nov had agreed to renew the Supreme Court, but brought no electoral-council renewal, election date or prisoner releases, with Foro Penal still counting 321. Washington’s security embrace of Rodríguez before any vote sharpens that contest, and the partnered model remains the most transferable lesson at Medium adaptability.

timeline.text: Three PLAN warships, including two Type 022 missile boats, and five China Coast Guard cutters intercepted the MV Lapu-Lapu resupply run about 60 nautical miles from Second Thomas Shoal, a warship radioed that it would take 'compulsory measures' and the mission was suspended, the first blocked run since the July 2024 understanding.

A China Coast Guard cutter trained its water cannon on BRP Cabra during a medical evacuation from BRP Sierra Madre, forcing a small-boat transfer four nautical miles off the reef that delayed the mission by nearly ten hours, while a PLA Navy frigate stood nearby.

The armed forces completed a rotation-and-resupply run to BRP Sierra Madre without incident, the first since the 24 September interception, while China's coast guard said it had approved and monitored the delivery and Manila denied seeking any permission; the same day PLA Navy ships shadowed USS Charleston near Sabina Shoal.

The carrier Liaoning and three destroyers sailed through the Sulu Sea and the Basilan Strait inside the Philippine archipelago, shadowed by Philippine warships, before heading east toward the Philippine Sea, as Chinese navy ships near Philippine-held features rose to 26 in the week to 26 October.

China's Southern Theater Command said its naval and air forces flew combat-readiness patrols around Scarborough Shoal as a countermeasure to Philippine 'provocations', a day after a Philippine patrol flight found an unidentified Chinese vessel with a sensor-fitted craft inside the shoal's lagoon.

The Philippine foreign ministry publicly rebuked unnamed officials and agencies for comments on China, saying all must align with the President's policy and that transparency cannot substitute for statecraft.

ASEAN and China failed to conclude the South China Sea code of conduct at the Manila summit despite about 80% of the draft being agreed, leaving its legal force and geographic scope to Singapore's 2027 chairmanship.
Satellite analysis reported by AFP showed China building a runway of nearly three kilometres on Antelope Reef in the Paracels, its second in that group and expected to be usable by mid-2027.

text: On grey-zone maritime coercion versus presence and resilience, the Established · Contested status holds in a restrained form: no collision, water-cannon use or blocked resupply was reported between 6 and 20 Nov, the last weekly count (10 Nov) put Chinese hulls at 29 across four features, and on 16 Nov ASEAN and China drafted a pledge of self-restraint while leaving the code's legal force and scope open, so coercion is paused rather than renounced. On maritime domain awareness versus ambiguous attribution, the Rising status is borne out from outside Manila: the Quad leaders announced a maritime patrol aircraft exercise on 17 Nov, and on 18 Nov satellite analysis exposed a near three-kilometre runway on Antelope Reef that Beijing calls civilian, so open-source imagery rather than state attribution is carrying the warning load.

On distributed maritime posture versus force protection, the Rising · Contested status is reinforced at theatre scale: a second Paracels runway, usable by mid-2027 and able to take fighters and bombers according to analysts quoted on 18 Nov, would extend land-based air cover over the northern sea lanes and make dispersed Philippine and Vietnamese outposts easier to watch and pressure. The quiet summit week lowers near-term clash risk without reducing that structural advantage, and adaptability stays Medium.

Taiwan's defence minister said the carrier Liaoning and other Chinese naval formations were conducting area-denial drills in the Western Pacific, although Beijing had declared no exercise.
Xi Jinping said reunification with Taiwan will certainly be realised, and Taiwan reported 29 Chinese military aircraft on a joint combat readiness patrol with warships.
Two Russian military aircraft flew through the air defence zone east of Taiwan after violating Japanese airspace off Okinoshima, on the eve of Putin's arrival in China for APEC.

On C2 and critical-infrastructure resilience versus isolation risk, the Rising status is borne out in the legal domain: on 17 Nov Washington asked the ICAO Council to rule that states managing high-seas flight regions cannot revoke Taiwanese overflights for political ends, showing isolation pursued through airspace administration as well as force. India's Border Security Force shoots dead two Pakistani men on the Punjab border, which India calls an infiltration attempt and Pakistan an unprovoked killing of villagers, and each side summons the other's envoy the next day.

Pakistan's Army Rocket Force Command test-fired the Fatah-2 Extended Range, billed as a hypersonic ballistic missile able to defeat missile defences, a week after testing an extended-range Fatah-4 cruise missile on 6 October.

text: On cross-border strike and counterstrike versus escalation management, the Established · Contested status is again only half borne out: no cross-LoC fire or lethal border incident was found after 17 Oct, and Pakistan’s confirmation on 19 Nov that Musadik Malik will attend the SCO forum in Delhi, with no bilateral meeting planned, shows contact resuming only under multilateral cover. On counterterrorism versus interstate deterrence, the Established status holds in its trigger form: the 11 Nov attack that wounded three CRPF personnel in Kulgam led to a week-long cordon, an associate killed at Laroo on 16 Nov and Lashkar commander Lateef Bhat killed in a mosque on 18 Nov, which Delhi framed as the end of the group’s local cadre. That shifts residual risk toward infiltrated foreign fighters, the attribution path that turned Pahalgam into an interstate crisis.

On air, missile and information operations versus nuclear-threshold ambiguity, the Contested status is quieter: no test was found after the Pralay trial of 5 Nov, and signalling moved to statements, with India’s Navy chief saying on 16 Nov that over 85% of Pakistan’s hardware is Chinese and that eight incoming submarines need watching (single source). Adaptability stays High; observed adaptation is incremental.

timeline.text: The military launches 'Operation 4926', a combined land, naval and air offensive against the Arakan Army across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, Kyaukphyu and Gwa townships in Rakhine State.
Six fibre-optic FPV drones strike Tada-U airbase near Mandalay; resistance says Yak-130 jets were hit, the junta says all were intercepted, and international flights are cancelled.

Junta warships, artillery and aircraft begin a week of failed landing attempts on Ngapyi Island opposite the Shwe Min Gan naval base near Sittwe, and by 14 October the Arakan Army still holds the island and has taken outposts on the city's edge, by local accounts.

The Arakan Army reportedly struck three navy vessels, including a frigate, near the Kaladan river mouth by the Shwe Min Gan naval base off Sittwe, sinking two, by anonymous military and AA-side accounts.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed a school and homes in Nyaung Pin Lay village in Sagaing, killing 11 people including four children, after a resistance warning could not reach the village because it had no internet.

State media said the army had taken the resistance government's special region military command headquarters, a Karen battalion headquarters and about ten other bases on the Mon–Bago border in a six-day operation.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila kept Myanmar's leader and foreign minister barred from summits and adopted a phased, progress-based engagement that may gradually restore full representation; on 18 November Min Aung Hlaing said his government would review relations with the bloc.
The International Court of Justice ruled 9–6 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017 and ordered prosecutions, safe return and compensation.

text: On distributed resistance versus state airpower, the Established · Contested status holds with the regime pressing harder from the air than on the ground: after the claimed Mon–Bago capture on 10 Nov (state media, unconfirmed), no ground change was reported near Sittwe, while a jet strike on 13 Nov killed 12 at the Byar La displacement camp in Ponnagyun, a camp residents had thought safe. Airpower is punishing the Arakan Army's rear population rather than breaking its siege lines. On commercial UAS and improvised systems versus conventional advantage, the Rising status is not contradicted but drew no new dated evidence this week beyond the 7 Nov gyrocopter strike in Sagaing (single source); diffusion is assumed, not newly shown.

On fragmented governance versus logistics and civilian resilience, the Established status is reinforced on its legitimacy side: ASEAN on 15 Nov kept Myanmar's leaders out and tied any return to progress, Min Aung Hlaing replied on 18 Nov that he would review ties, and on 19 Nov the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide and ordered safe Rohingya return. The regime's governance claim now faces a binding judgment as well as regional conditionality. Adaptability stays High.

items.whyNow: The Houthis now hold the Yemeni coast west of Aden and are pressing on the last defensible line before the city, while their salvos at Riyadh and claims against the East-West pipeline, the main Gulf export route around a closed Hormuz, continue. Losing Aden or the Bab al-Mandeb shore would put both Gulf bypass routes that matter to Singapore's energy and shipping under Houthi threat.
changes: 18 Nov: Saudi forces said they intercepted three Houthi cruise missiles and drones near Riyadh over 17–18 Nov and another drone over the south; Critical Threats judged these aimed at Saudi critical infrastructure to press Riyadh to end operations and meet Houthi economic demands (Critical Threats).

17 Nov: The Houthis claimed drone strikes on two East-West pipeline pumping stations in Riyadh province and a radar at Sharurah, which could not be verified; Yemen's army claimed 661 attacks and 173 Houthi casualties in its 'Dawn of Yemen' campaign, and parliament voted to designate the Houthis a terrorist group; in Iraq, sources said Prime Minister al-Zaydi and Quds Force chief Ghaani agreed on a Kataib Hezbollah withdrawal from Jurf al-Sakhr (Critical Threats, Al Jazeera).

16 Nov: Five military sources told Reuters the Houthis reached Khawr Umayrah, about 100 km west of Aden, after government forces 'redeployed' from positions near Bab al-Mandeb; the Houthis took Dhubab airport and a position near Jabal Kharaz, Saudi Arabia replaced its joint forces commander with Fayyad al-Ruwaili, and Iraq ordered its army toward Jurf al-Sakhr with a 20 Nov deadline (Shafaq/Reuters, Critical Threats, Al Jazeera).

15 Nov: The coalition said it intercepted two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and three drones in the Eastern region, the Houthis claimed missiles at Riyadh's airport and financial centre and at Saudi-backed troops in Lahij, and the US embassy issued a nationwide alert; Saudi authorities count at least 26 dead from Houthi attacks since 23 Sep (Al Jazeera, Shafaq News).
14 Nov: Baghdad said its investigation linked Kataib Hezbollah to oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhr, setting up the government's move against the militia stronghold (Critical Threats).

timeline.text: The Houthis declare a naval and air blockade of Saudi Arabia in response to a strike on Sanaa airport, ending four years of relative calm under the 2022 truce.
Drones launched from Iraq's Maysan province hit Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline in Riyadh and Medina provinces; Riyadh shuts the line the next day and Brent tops $100.
Houthi forces seize Perim Island and the last stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast a day after taking Mocha, gaining control of Bab al-Mandab and reiterating a ban on Saudi ships.

A Houthi missile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid airport, killing 12 people and wounding 309 by Saudi count, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade, and the airport was shut.
Houthi forces took Souq al-Rabouh and heights in Lahij's al-Maqatira district, coming within about 80 km of Aden, their closest approach since 2015, by the account of four military sources.

Debris from an intercepted Houthi attack damaged Aramco's office tower in Riyadh, and a drone launched from Iraq's Salahuddin area halted the Khor Mor gas field in Kurdistan, cutting about 2.8 gigawatts of power.
A Houthi strike set a limited fire on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, Riyadh moved schools online, and Syria confirmed it is sending about 600 special forces to the kingdom.
Government forces pulled back from positions near Bab al-Mandeb and the Houthis reached Khawr Umayrah, about 100 km west of Aden, as Saudi Arabia replaced its joint forces commander.

text: Long-range attack versus layered protection (Rising · Contested) is borne out, with defence now holding better than the week before: Saudi forces reported intercepting two ballistic missiles over Riyadh on 15 Nov and three cruise missiles and drones on 17–18 Nov, and the Houthi claims against East-West pipeline pumping stations on 16–17 Nov remain unverified, although the US embassy's nationwide alert on 15 Nov shows the threat is still driving protective measures. Maritime disruption versus route resilience (Established · Contested) is contradicted at sea, with no corroborated merchant-ship attack, but strengthened ashore: government forces left positions near Bab al-Mandeb and the Houthis reached Khawr Umayrah, about 100 km west of Aden, on 16 Nov, putting more of the strait's shore under Houthi control.

Regional basing versus militia targeting (Established · Contested) is borne out on two fronts. Riyadh replaced its joint forces commander on 16 Nov as the Jabal Kharaz line before Aden came under pressure (single source for the capture there), and in Iraq Baghdad moved troops toward Kataib Hezbollah's Jurf al-Sakhr with a 20 Nov deadline, testing host-nation control of militias. Adaptability is High on the first topic and Medium on the other two.
